facts.text: C.H.U.D. cost just $1.25 million to make and grossed about $4.65 million, a healthy profit for a sewer-monster movie.
Laure Mattos, who plays the first victim, Flora Bosch, is the real-life wife of co-star Daniel Stern, who plays the Reverend.
C.H.U.D. officially means "Cannibalistic Humanoid Underground Dweller", but the toxic-waste crates in the film also read "Contamination Hazard Urban Disposal", if you can make out the print.
Joe Bob Briggs opened The Last Drive-In's first-ever episode with C.H.U.D. After it, he cracked: "It's five seconds of monsters, two hours of smug theater actors."
Jordan Peele's 2019 horror film Us opens on a shot that includes a VHS copy of C.H.U.D. The film was part of his inspiration.
Jordan Peele has said his first girlfriend was the daughter of C.H.U.D. director Douglas Cheek. He first saw the film around age 11 or 12.
Stars Christopher Curry (Captain Bosch) and Daniel Stern (the Reverend) have claimed they rewrote more than half of Parnell Hall's script. Nerdist also describes the production as full of turmoil.
C.H.U.D. was the only feature directed by Douglas Cheek, who was primarily a film editor.
C.H.U.D. was announced in 1980 with Douglas Netter producing and Richard Compton attached to direct a script by Stephen Abbott. It reached the screen four years later under different hands.
Creature effects artist John Caglione Jr. designed the C.H.U.D.s. His early concept art gave them much more animal-like faces than the final monsters.
Some posters opened with a fake preamble: a New York paper had reported colonies of people living under the city, but "the paper was incorrect. What is living under the city is not human."
In 1985 an urban legend claimed C.H.U.D. was based on a true story from 1970s Cincinnati. It was proven false.
C.H.U.D. was Kim Greist's first movie. She went on to play the angel in Terry Gilliam's Brazil and William Petersen's wife in Manhunter.
C.H.U.D. was the film debut of Christopher Curry (Captain Bosch). He later played Rico's father in Starship Troopers.
Mondo Digital's review sees C.H.U.D. as building on Gary Sherman's British cult film Raw Meat (1972), which also had cannibals living in subway tunnels, with a toxic-spill twist.
The black beeper box used in the film to retrieve answering-machine messages was cutting-edge 1980s tech. Callers dialed their own number and the tone unlocked playback.
The film's opening street scene was shot on Crosby Street in SoHo, just south of Broome Street. Several of the "skid row" scenes were filmed a few doors away on the same block.
C.H.U.D. opened August 1984 at #13 at the box office, with $1.76 million from 310 theaters. It fell to #14 in week two.
The New York Times' Lawrence Van Gelder called C.H.U.D. "light commercial entertainment" and "a praiseworthy effort" among horror films.
Keith Phipps of The A.V. Club wrote that C.H.U.D. is "perfect for bleary-eyed late-night viewing and pretty much unwatchable at any other hour."
Manhattan's soup kitchen is actually in New Jersey: it was filmed at North Baptist Church in Jersey City, a building gutted by fire in 1978 that reopened in 1985 under a new name.
Time Out New York's Joshua Rothkopf put C.H.U.D. on its list of best New York-set films, calling it "more funny than scary."
Martin Cooper's score for C.H.U.D. was later ranked number 33 on Rolling Stone's list of the 35 Greatest Horror Soundtracks.
On April Fools' Day 2011, the Criterion Collection announced a C.H.U.D. edition as spine #573. It was a joke, but Arrow Video issued a real special-edition Blu-ray in 2016.
The diner used in the film was the real Cleveland Diner at 114 Kenmare Street in Manhattan. It is now a restaurant called La Esquina.
Since late 2019 the word "chud" has become internet slang used to mock far-right users, taken from this film's monsters.
Cordis Heard, who has a supporting role in C.H.U.D., is the sister of the film's star John Heard (photographer George Cooper).
C.H.U.D. has been referenced in The Simpsons, Clerks II, Futurama, Archer, Rick and Morty and Donnie Darko, among others.
The 2003 video game Tony Hawk's Underground includes a nod to the film under the name T.H.U.D.
The movie's police station exterior is the real 9th Precinct on East 5th Street in the East Village. The reverse shot was filmed at Spring and Mercer in SoHo.
The 1989 sequel, C.H.U.D. II: Bud the C.H.U.D., swapped the sewer monsters for a comedic zombie.
Home video offers a 96-minute "Integral Cut", previously seen only on network TV, with the gore restored. It adds scenes such as Lauren discussing her pregnancy with her boyfriend.
Blumhouse's Ryan Turek compared C.H.U.D. to a Larry Cohen movie (the It's Alive director) on the Shock Waves podcast. Mondo Digital agrees but says it lacks Cohen's sly humor.
C.H.U.D. was shot entirely in New York City, reportedly in fall 1983, with locations including SoHo, Central Park, San Remo Towers and the Chambers Street subway station.
John Heard (George Cooper) earned a 1999 Emmy nomination for playing corrupt detective Vin Makazian on The Sopranos.
Producer Andrew Bonime told Fangoria (issue 32) that C.H.U.D. was "an expensive looking film and an expensive concept" and "a high quality kind of picture."
Dread Central has called the film Bunker Heights a spiritual successor to C.H.U.D.
C.H.U.D. was a theatrical disappointment but turned into a success on video and cable. Media Home Entertainment released it on VHS and Betamax in 1984.
Joe Bob Briggs, hosting The Last Drive-In, said Daniel Stern's soup-kitchen Reverend looks creepier than the mutants. He also joked that Ernie from Sesame Street would make a better C.H.U.D.
C.H.U.D. is one of John Goodman's first movie appearances. He plays a cop, in a role Jay Thomas, a Mork & Mindy regular, shares with him.
Joe Bob Briggs gave C.H.U.D. two stars on The Last Drive-In. He called Kim Greist's shower scene, built around a clogged drain, the least sexy in film history.
Not everyone's a fan: a review on The Stop Button gave C.H.U.D. zero out of four stars, calling the cast stronger than the material and saying the script lacks suspense.
